We are proud of our...
Welcome to our school
I hope that our pupils, their families and professional colleagues will find the website interesting and informative.
At Lady Margaret Primary School we provide rich and engaging learning experiences which create life long memories. Our curriculum has been designed, by our staff, with careful consideration of the sequence of content necessary for pupils to make progress and respect for cultural diversity.
Our highly motivated staff team provide our pupils with the knowledge they need for subsequent learning and prepare them well for the next stage of their education. We are committed to UNICEF’s Rights of the Child and prepare our learners for life in modern Britain, encouraging responsibility, respect and tolerance.
We believe that a rich balanced curriculum is the heritage and entitlement of every child. Literature and Oracy are our cornerstone. Via wonderful stories, poems and non-fiction, pupils discover new horizons and imagine faraway places, times and situations. We are privileged to serve a community with a diverse cultural heritage, and this inspires and enriches the global perspective of our curriculum.
Key to our work is building positive relationships with parents and families, to ensure pupils have every opportunity to progress in a happy and supportive learning environment.
Our school is part of the growing Ealing Bridges Federation as we are committed to collaborative work and the sharing of best practice amongst schools. Through the federation our pupils develop relationships and share experiences with pupils from other schools, which supports their personal development and preparation for the next stage of their education.
The Headteacher, Miss Simpson and I look forward to welcoming you into our school.
Helen Rai
Executive Headteacher MA, NPQEL
Liane Simpson

pageCache.pageTitle: Aims and Visions - Lady Margaret Primary School
pageCache.text:
Mission Statement
Children learn best when happy. Their learning environment must be as engaging, vibrant and supportive as possible. We are a highly inclusive school and are committed to ensuring every child reaches their full potential and leaves our school with inspiring lifelong memories.
Vision Statement
We focus on developing staff knowledge and expertise to provide the best start to a child's educational journey. We deliver a knowledge rich, engaging and aspirational curriculum, with a wealth of extra-curricular experiences that are enriching and inspirational. This reflects our high expectations and the excellence our children deserve.
Core Values
Our values describe the approach to teaching and learning which we use to develop pupils and prepare them for future life.
LEARNING
Learning describes our educational ethos. Our focus is on enriching children’s lives and celebrating the diversity of the community. We achieve this by providing a wide and rich set of learning experiences, coherently linked to our curriculum which fully engage children and bring learning to life.
MOTIVATION
Learning describes our educational ethos. Our focus is on enriching children’s lives and celebrating the diversity of the community. We achieve this by providing a wide and rich set of learning experiences, coherently linked to our curriculum which fully engage children and bring learning to life.
PROGRESS
Progression summarises how our curriculum is coherently designed to support learning ensuring cumulative development of knowledge and skills as children move through the school. It supports children to master core concepts and develop deep understanding.
SUCCESS
Success describes how we bring out the best in every child, recognising needs, talents and interests, and set ourselves the highest standards.
Part of Ealing Bridges Federation

pageCache.pageTitle: Personal Development and Wellbeing - Lady Margaret Primary School
pageCache.text:
Personal development and wellbeing
My Chronicles: A Journey of Experience and Reflection
Mental health
We understand that positive mental health is fundamental to our pupils overall wellbeing and success. That is why we prioritise mental health support at every step of our pupils’ journey. Through our partnership with the Schools Counselling Partnership and THRIVE, we provide a safe space for children to express themselves, process emotions, and develop coping strategies.
We believe that by fostering a culture of openness and understanding, we can break down the stigma surrounding mental health and empower our pupils to prioritise their emotional wellbeing. Whether it is through one-on-one counselling sessions, group activities, or mindfulness exercises, we strive to instil resilience and promote a positive mindset in every child.
Rights Respecting
At our school, we proudly hold the prestigious title of a Gold Rights Respecting School, where every child’s rights are not just recognised, but celebrated and protected. Pupils here confidently discuss a range of rights and understand their importance in their lives and the wider world.
Our commitment to children’s rights is ingrained in every aspect of our school culture, with rights prominently displayed across our curriculum and communication channels. Through our dedicated leadership and ongoing staff training, we ensure that the principles of the Rights Respecting School Award are woven into the fabric of our daily interactions and learning experiences.
Through workshops, newsletters, and regular communication, we ensure that families are well-informed and engaged in our work on children’s rights. Together, we strive to create a nurturing and inclusive community where every child’s rights are respected, protected, and upheld.
Highlights from our January 2023 gold report:
Our school is like a big family where everyone’s rights are respected, and we learn together how to make the world a better place.
When I see the Morality Ambassadors helping others on the playground, it makes me feel like we’re all part of something special, where kindness and respect are the norm.
I love how our teachers protect our rights. If there’s any bullying, they deal with it immediately, making us feel safe and cared for.
– A heartening sentiment expressed by a pupil, highlighting the supportive environment nurtured by the school staff.
Pupil voice
At our school, pupils are empowered to direct their own learning and voice their opinions. From creating and directing their own films to suggesting improvements to their lessons, children play an active role in shaping their educational experience. Through oracy-focused activities and rights-based language development, we foster a culture where children feel confident to speak up and advocate for themselves and others.
Inclusivity
Our commitment to diversity and inclusion is reflected in our curriculum, which is regularly reviewed and developed to represent the rich tapestry of our school community. Children with Special Educational Needs receive tailored support, ensuring that every child has the opportunity to reach their full potential.
OPAL
At our school, we believe in the power of outdoor play and learning to foster creativity, resilience, and teamwork. Through our OPAL (Outdoor Play and Learning) program, we’ve transformed our playground into a vibrant space where children can explore, imagine, and connect with nature. From the ‘theatre’ to the sandpit, every corner of our outdoor area is designed to inspire curiosity and adventure.
Thanks to generous donations, we’ve been able to enhance our playing opportunities even further, creating new areas for child-led learning and discovery. Whether they’re building dens, digging in the mud kitchen, or collaborating on imaginative games, our students benefit from the freedom and joy that comes with outdoor play. The OPAL program not only promotes physical activity and well-being but also cultivates important life skills such as problem-solving, communication, and resilience.
Through outdoor play, our pupils learn valuable lessons that will stay with them for a lifetime, shaping them into confident and compassionate individuals.
Assemblies
Assemblies at our school serve as meaningful gatherings where our community comes together to celebrate achievements, reflect on values, and foster a sense of belonging. Each assembly serves a unique purpose tailored to support our pupils’ holistic development. Singing assemblies ignite joy and camaraderie as voices unite in song, uplifting spirits and nurturing a sense of togetherness.
Head of School assemblies provide opportunities for leadership, where students share updates, achievements, and inspirational messages, fostering a culture of responsibility and empowerment. Pastoral assemblies offer a space for reflection and support, addressing topics such as well-being, resilience, and kindness, equipping students with the tools to navigate life’s challenges with confidence and compassion. Race equality and diversity assemblies promote understanding and appreciation of different cultures, fostering an inclusive environment where every child feels valued and respected.
Through these diverse assemblies, we not only cultivate a strong sense of community but also instil values that will guide our students to become compassionate, responsible, and respectful individuals, ready to make a positive impact on the world around them.
In summary, the federation is a nurturing community dedicated to holistic development. From promoting positive mental health and fostering inclusivity to upholding children’s rights and offering enriching programs like OPAL and diverse assemblies, we aim to cultivate confident, resilient, and compassionate individuals. With the support of our staff and school community, we empower every child to thrive academically, emotionally, and socially, preparing them to make a positive impact in the world.
Part of Ealing Bridges Federation

School Opening Hours
The compulsory school day
At Lady Margaret Primary School, the compulsory school day begins with registration at 8.45 am and ends at 3.15 pm when pupils go home.
In line with DfE requirements, in a typical school week pupils are at school for 32 hours and 30 minutes.
This does not include any extra curricular activities that a pupil may choose to participate in.
The normal school day is broken down as follows:
At LMPS we offer a soft start to the school day, this means that children can come into class from 8.35 am which gives them time to settle down and prepare for the school day.

pageCache.pageTitle: Our Curriculum - Lady Margaret Primary School
pageCache.text:
Our Curriculum
Linked to our value of Learning, our curriculum in a "carefully crafted journey" - ambitious, inclusive, and routed in the belief that every child can thrive. Through expert teaching and purposeful sequencing , we build strong foundations, deepen understanding, and ignite curiosity. We have four curriculum themes; LEGACY, MORALITY, POWER and SUSTAINABILITY, which provide meaningful links between subjects and subject specific concepts.
Our curriculum vision
Our curriculum exceeds the national curriculum expectations. It is designed around high quality texts which have been carefully selected, taking into account the community we serve. The curriculum is knowledge rich and coherently sequenced to enable our pupils to build their understanding of key concepts in each specific subject over time. We aim to develop a thirst for learning which will remain with our pupils for life. The development of effective communication skills, vocabulary development and use of technology are embedded into the curriculum.
Keeping stakeholders informed
Valuable information is shared with parents on a regular basis through our half termly curriculum newsletters and the parent overviews. We formally report to parents, on the impact of the curriculum on their child’s progress, six times a year. We seek their views termly through surveys and workshops.
Leaders work with governors to review the impact of the curriculum and the provision for vulnerable pupils.
We place pupil voice front and centre of our review methodology, frequently and systematically asking them to share their view of the curriculum and their engagement in learning.
Curriculum specific Occupational Therapy Integration
Lady Margaret Primary School is committed to embedding Occupational Therapy (OT) strategies across the curriculum to ensure every child can access learning, regulate their emotions and develop independence.
We believe that inclusive, sensory-aware environments and OT-informed teaching practices empower pupils to thrive academically, socially and emotionally. Our OT approach aligns with the principles of universal inclusive practice, ensuring that adaptations and supports are available to all pupils, not just those with identified learning needs. OT strategies are integrated through a graduated approach—universal, targeted and specialist—supporting pupils at every level of need. We promote emotional regulation, sensory processing awareness and motor skill development as foundational to learning and participation.
Part of Ealing Bridges Federation

Music
The curriculum for music enriches creative confidence and cultural understanding. They develop key musical skills; listen, appraise, compose and perform. They build a strong foundation in rhythm melody and notation. Though singing and playing instruments we encourage self expression and creativity and hope children discover the joy that music can bring and understand the diversity of music from a range of cultures.
Music is a universal language that embodies one of the highest forms of creativity. A high quality music education should engage and inspire pupils to develop a love of music and their talent as musicians, and so increase their self-confidence, creativity and sense of achievement.
Our music curriculum inspires every pupil to develop a love of music and their talent as a musician.
Music is used to increase self-confidence and creativity as pupils perform in class, year, key stage and whole school assemblies for a variety of audiences.
As pupils progress, they should develop a critical engagement with music, allowing them to compose, and to listen with discrimination to the best in the musical canon.
The national curriculum for music aims to ensure that all pupils:
At Lady Margaret Primary School, we offer an exciting and engaging range of extra-curricular opportunities outside of the pupils’ structured music education:
This is about all the other musical events and opportunities that we organise, such as singing in assembly, concerts and shows, and trips to professional concerts.
Reading Notation: Pulse & Rhythm
• Confidently read and perform rhythms with a wide range of note values, including semibreves, minims, crotchets, quavers, semiquavers and their equivalent rests, fluently interpreting rhythm patterns and note durations.• Sight-read and perform intricate rhythmic phrases and rhythms from prepared notation, confidently maintaining accurate timing and rhythm throughout, in an ensemble of up to 4 parts.
Reading Notation: Pitch
• Fluently read and perform pitch notation within an octave range (e.g. C–C).• Interpret and perform music with dynamics and articulation.
Singing and Performing
• Sing a broad range of songs, including those with complex rhythms and harmonies, with a strong sense of ensemble and performance.• Perform three – and four – part rounds, partner songs, and songs with intricate structures.
Instrumental Performance
• Play complex melodies and accompaniments following staff notation, utilising a wide range of notes within an octave (do – do), whilst contributing to the interpretation and expression of the music.• Accompany melodies using block chords or a bass line using keyboards, tuned percussion or melodic instruments.• Demonstrate proficiency in playing by ear, copying longer phrases and complex melodies on tuned instruments
Composition and Improvisation
• Extend improvisation skills through working in small groups to create music with multiple sections, repetition, and contrast.• Compose melodies made from pairs of phrases, in a major or minor key suitable for the instrument chosen, enhanced with rhythmic or chordal accompaniment.• Plan and compose an 8- or 16-beat melodic phrase using the pentatonic scale and incorporate rhythmic variety.

Science
The teaching of science helps children to develop useful knowledge, skills and attitudes about the world we live in. The curriculum is designed for conceptual progression, and there is a strong emphasis on scientific vocabulary. Pupils regularly engage in investigative work developing their own hypotheses and drawing conclusions. We gained the Science Quality Mark for our excellent teaching of science. The subject is taught by a specialist.
In the modern world in which we live today, science touches every part of our lives. Our future prosperity depends on scientific advances and yet we have a shortage of scientists.
At Lady Margaret Primary School, we celebrate and promote science, both in science specific lessons, and across the curriculum. Our pupils share a sense of excitement and curiosity about the natural world in which we live.
They also develop the belief that if they are not sure about something, they should not accept it, but challenge and ask WHY?
Because all pupils are scientists, they answer the question why, by:
As a result, our curriculum is structured to ensure that our learning is developed through: observing, investigating and researching.
Our aim is pupils will be so inspired by Science at Lady Margaret Primary School, they will become the greatly needed scientists of tomorrow.
Science curriculum follows the National Curriculum themes and requirements, whilst also linking to our class topics so as to provide a meaningful context for learning.
Science is covered in the Foundation Stage through ‘Understanding the World’. Here, pupils explore and investigate the natural world as well as themselves.
Throughout Key stages 1 and 2, key learning is reinforced and developed through a combination of: investigation, experimentation, research and observation.
Children are encouraged to question, predict and test their ideas through whole class, group or individual investigations and project work and then form conclusions. Thus developing a curiosity and a desire for learning.
As science is everywhere, this is reflected in our wider curriculum, which has many cross curricular links to science planned in.
Our commitment to science at Lady Margaret School is reflected in our investment of a specialist science teacher who both teaches and supports teachers in the delivery of science.
Science is not just limited to the classroom. During their time at LMPS, children widen their experiences by participating in educational visits. Examples of these include the Science Museum, the Wetland Centre, Kew Gardens and Odds Farm.
In addition, there are a number of after school clubs that pupils are able to attend. These are designed to enable pupils to have a greater input into what they study. For example, in one current club, pupils are combining their electrical, DT and programming skills to construct a haunted house that is wired up with motors, lights, and servos to create a variety of spooky effects.
All the pupils are involved in the development and running of our edible garden, which was a winner in ‘The Ealing in bloom award’. This develops a greater understanding of the life cycles of plant life, and also the importance of plants for us.
Early years also develop their understanding of the lifecycle each year, when they observe the hatching of chicks. Some of the chickens join the hens which reside by the wildlife garden. Once again the pupils are encouraged to visit and observe our chickens, who are now quite tame.
Finally, we are developing an outdoor wildlife area to enable us to develop a better understanding of the wild life that is around us, that we are often not aware of.
Our aim is pupils will be so inspired by Science at Lady Margaret Primary School, they will become the greatly needed scientists of tomorrow.
When our pupils move on to High School we hope that many of them will continue in their studies of science.
Our pupils will have:
…developed a love and passion for the subject.
…have a good scientific knowledge and conceptual understanding of science.
…have the confidence and ability to carry out, and report on, science enquiries that help them to answer scientific questions about the world around them.
…be equipped with scientific knowledge required to understand the uses and implications of science, today and for the future.
…use their scientific knowledge and understanding to care for the world in which they live.

pageCache.pageTitle: Our Curriculum Enhancements - Lady Margaret Primary School
pageCache.text:
Our Curriculum Enhancements
KIT Theatre
Our children all have opportunities, throughout their time at Lady Margaret, to take part in immersive theatre which brings the stories they learn to life and deepens their understanding.
This is an integral part of our Oracy curriculum, providing the experience of working and performing with professional actors. The projects each year support critical thinking, dialogue, role play and collaboration, helping pupils articulate ideas and practice effective communication.
Primary Shakespeare Company
Primary Shakespeare Company brings Shakespeare's plays to life, through drama, storytelling and performance, working alongside professional actors. It enhances pupil's oracy by fostering speaking and listening skills and encouraging creative expression. This project is part of our year 4 curriculum, exposing pupils to the classic stories and Shakespearean language. Our pupils have the opportunity to perform, alongside other schools, in a real theatre. This provides an opportunity for performance but also critical review of others' performance.
In 2024, the Primary Shakespeare Company awarded Lady Margaret the Annie Williams trophy for their impressive work and performance of Julius Caesar. As a result of winning this prestigious award, pupils visited the House of Lords to share experiences of the project and met Baroness Estelle Morris. Pupils also presented to board members of the John Lyon's Charity which supports this superb project.
HeyDay UK
In year 5 our pupils have an opportunity to work alongside professional filmmakers. Our pupils are empowered to create their own films, working on scripting, filming and editing. It enhances pupils oracy and confidence by developing skills in storytelling, scriptwriting, collaborative discussions and performance. The project fosters creativity, confidence building and effective communication through the filmmaking process.
As part of our wonderful work with Heyday, pupils are invited to attend the British Film Institute (BFI) for an interschool short film festival. This event celebrates our achievements and budding filmmaking skills. Pupils are provided with a platform to speak about their films and the many diverse themes they encapsulate.
EveryDay Magic
Everyday Magic's professional storytellers bring songs, rhymes and stories to life with our youngest children. It helps to develop children's oracy, by developing active participation in storytelling and performance which builds confidence and develops language.
The stories fire up imagination and excitement and introduce both familiar and new ideas.
Forest School Association
We run our Forest School on the fields, amongst the trees and plants at our partner school site. We have a trained member of staff on our team who runs weekly Forest School sessions for our children in year 1 and Reception. In addition, we hold Forest School for all our children throughout the year.
This programme supports play, exploration and supported risk taking. It develops confidence and self esteem through hands-on activities in the natural environment and is closely linked to our theme of sustainability as children are taught about how to look after our natural world.
Trees For Cities - Edible Playground
Our edible playground was created in partnership with Trees for Cities in 2014. Our children's experience of cultivating food and maintaining the growing area, has developed over the past ten years. Children are involved in the planning, growing plants from seeds, planting out, managing plots and harvesting fruit and vegetables. Children have raised money for new seeds and garden development by selling small plants grown from seeds and vegetables to members of our community.
They regularly take part in projects which develop their understanding of the natural world such as growing seeds that were taken to space, which involved Tim Peake, the renowned British European Space Agency Astronaut. We annually enter, and usually win, the Ealing in Bloom competition and in 2024 we won the Cultivating Ealing School Gardens competition for the best overall school garden. This is linked to our theme of sustainability.
Music Provision
Music is a key element of our curriculum entitlement for all pupils and is provided by music specialists. In addition to weekly music lessons, we also ensure that every child learns and instrument whilst at Lady Margaret.
In year 4, there is an African drumming programme which provides a dynamic platform to enhance skills by emphasising rhythm collaboration and expressive communication.
Through call and response patterns, our pupils develop active listening and an understanding of musical rhythm. In year 5, all pupils learn to play the ukulele, learning how to pluck and strum, and elements of reading music.
In addition, we have a school choir, who regularly perform within the community, but also do an annual visit to an inter-school performance at the Royal Albert Hall. We also have I-Rock that provides small group tuition to children with a particular interest.
In 2025 we are taking pupils to the open air opera at Holland Park, where the importance of music to enhance our lives will be illustrated. Through the music curriculum our pupils are exposed to a range of musical artist and their legacy. We are always looking for opportunities for our most talented pupils to develop their skills outside of school.
Artist In Residence
Alongside our outstanding art curriculum, we run an annual artist in residence programme for selected pupils, who show talent and or particular interest in art, from each year group to work with an artist, in order to develop their skills further and ignite their passion for the subject.
This further enhances their understanding of the legacy of artists, past and present
Clubs
We have a wide range of clubs, which run after school every day. Many are linked to sports and fitness, led by sports specialist and leading to high achievement in sports.
Whilst our children are exposed to a wide range of sports and practice on sports' fields with high quality equipment, our specialist sport is cricket and we have professional cricket nets for children to practice in. We are always looking for opportunities for our most talented pupils to develop their skills outside of school.
In addition, we have an after school and before school club and many additional "booster" classes to ensure pupils keep up academically.
Animal Care
Lady Margaret has a school dog called Kenny, along with resident chickens and ducks. Children are taught about these animals, their needs and behaviours. This develops a sense of care, responsibility and respect for the welfare of living things. Children in Nursery and Reception have the opportunity to meet and learn about a wide range of farm animals during an annual mobile farm visit.
The school has recently developed a wild garden with a pond, bug hotels and wild flowers, to encourage a wide range of mini-beasts to take up residence. There are also swift boxes around the school to provide a safe environment for nesting swifts whose natural habitats are in decline.
Giving children opportunities to learn about the natural world and the importance of protecting and respecting the environment links to our themes of morality and sustainability.
Aspiration Day
The school holds an annual aspiration day for year 6 pupils. This event provides an opportunity for pupils to meet and interview a diverse group of professionals who volunteer their time.
The aim of this event is to broaden pupils' knowledge of different careers, raise their aspirations and develop an understanding of what skills each career requires. This event links to the theme of power.
Trips and educational visits
Parents will be asked to contribute to the additional costs of an event or visit which the school may incur. Unfortunately should we receive insufficient funds to cover these additional costs, the planned visit or event may not go ahead. Families who are experiencing financial hardship should contact the school and support may be available. Please refer to our Charges and Remissions Policy available in the policy section of this website.

Art & Design
Art and design is used not only as a form of communication but also as a form of expression. As artists, we explore some of the highest forms of creativity. We design, craft and invent our own art work using knowledge and skills. We understand the importance of art in history and culture and study famous artists and their importance.‘Every child is an artist. The problem is how we remain an artist when we grow up’ - Pablo Picasso
As artists, we explore some of the highest forms of creativity. We design, craft and invent our own art work using knowledge and skills. We understand the importance of art in history and culture and study famous artists and their importance.
‘Every child is an artist. The problem is how we remain an artist when we grow up’
At Lady Margaret Primary School, we teach Art and Design as a discrete subject that link to either the core text, or the focus topic for that half term (geography or history). This makes the learning memorable, meaningful and enjoyable while simultaneously developing a breadth of study of artistic knowledge and skills.
The learning journey in Art and Design consists of the following:
Our Art and Design curriculum, starting from the Early Years foundation stage up to Key Stage 2, is a culturally rich plan in order to expose our children to art in the wider world.
Our curriculum coverage allows for a breadth of opportunities such as the engagement in an artists in residence programme, Legacy Project and cultural week. Lady Margaret School serves a diverse community of many cultures and languages. We want all our children to gain knowledge and understanding of the art from around the world.
Throughout the academic year, our children have opportunities to further develop their understanding of artic knowledge and skills through other subjects such as PSHE (anti-bullying week), Reading (Book week), Religious Studies (Spirited arts competition) and much more.
Demonstrate secure artistic mastery
Pupils confidently control a broad range of media — including drawing, painting and sculpture — showing depth, fluency and increasing precision in their technique. Their work demonstrates the secure foundations needed for a successful transition into secondary art.
Apply a clearly sequenced body of artistic knowledge
They use an increasingly sophisticated visual language, showing strong understanding of colour, pattern, texture, line, shape, form and space. Their knowledge builds systematically over time, preventing gaps and supporting deep conceptual understanding.
Think and create like real artists
Pupils use sketchbooks purposefully to explore ideas, record observations, refine work over time and develop independence. Their artistic journey shows resilience, curiosity and the ability to improve work through thoughtful revision.
Evaluate artwork with confidence and accuracy
They analyse their own and others’ work using correct artistic terminology, communicating ideas with confidence. Their evaluations show insight, critical awareness and the ability to justify decisions.
Understand the cultural and historical significance of art
Pupils know a diverse range of influential artists, architects and designers. They recognise how art shapes, reflects and challenges society and can connect artistic movements, styles and ideas to their own creative decisions.
Produce creative, original and purposeful outcomes
Their final pieces show imagination, technical skill and thoughtful use of materials. They make informed artistic choices, work with increasing independence and take pride in high-quality outcomes that reflect sustained practice and personal expression.

Computing
The curriculum for computing aims to equip pupils with the skills and knowledge to thrive in a digital. They learn to use technology and a range of programmes, developing problem solving and logical reasoning techniques. We prioritise teaching pupils how to stay safe, respectful and informed online.
A high-quality computing education equips pupils to use computational thinking and creativity to understand and change the world. Computing has deep links with mathematics, science, and design and technology, and provides insights into both natural and artificial systems. The core of computing is computer science, in which pupils are taught the principles of information and computation, how digital systems work, and how to put this knowledge to use through programming. Building on this knowledge and understanding, pupils are equipped to use information technology to create programs, systems and a range of content. Computing also ensures that pupils become digitally literate – able to use, and express themselves and develop their ideas through, information and communication technology – at a level suitable for the future workplace and as active participants in a digital world.
The national curriculum for computing aims to ensure that all pupils:
• can understand and apply the fundamental principles and concepts of computer science, including abstraction, logic, algorithms and data representation
• can analyse problems in computational terms, and have repeated practical experience of writing computer programs in order to solve such problems
• can evaluate and apply information technology, including new or unfamiliar technologies, analytically to solve problems
• are responsible, competent, confident and creative users of information and communication technology.
KS1 Pupils should be taught to:
• understand what algorithms are; how they are implemented as programs on digital devices; and that programs execute by following precise and unambiguous instructions
• create and debug simple programs
• use logical reasoning to predict the behaviour of simple programs
• use technology purposefully to create, organise, store, manipulate and retrieve digital content
• recognise common uses of information technology beyond school
• use technology safely and respectfully, keeping personal information private; identify where to go for help and support when they have concerns about content or contact on the internet or other online technologies.
KS2Pupils should be taught to:
• design, write and debug programs that accomplish specific goals, including controlling or simulating physical systems; solve problems by decomposing them into smaller parts
• use sequence, selection, and repetition in programs; work with variables and various forms of input and output
• use logical reasoning to explain how some simple algorithms work and to detect and correct errors in algorithms and programs
• understand computer networks including the internet; how they can provide multiple services, such as the world wide web; and the opportunities they offer for communication and collaboration
• use search technologies effectively, appreciate how results are selected and ranked, and be discerning in evaluating digital content
• select, use and combine a variety of software (including internet services) on a range of digital devices to design and create a range of programs, systems and content that accomplish given goals, including collecting, analysing, evaluating and presenting data and information
• use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly; recognise acceptable / unacceptable behaviour; identify a range of ways to report concerns about content and contact.
The curriculum has been written to support all pupils, with units containing a number of scaffolding activities and utilising effective pedagogies to ensure high quality teaching. However, you may still need to adapt resources to enable some of your pupils, to access lessons fully.
The following principles will help you make adaptations that benefit all learners, and these will be more effective if you identify clearly what it is your individual pupils need help with – do they have poor working memory that means that following instructions is more difficult, or do they need help to stay focussed when completing projects?
Be safe, respectful and knowledgeable users of technology and the World Wide Web.
Be confident and competent users of a wide variety of software and hardware.
Recognise and appropriately use the vocabulary associated with technology including basic coding language.
Understand how technology has developed over time and continues to change according to demand and how they can use it to their advantage across all aspects of life and learning.

pageCache.text:
Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) Policy
Lady Margaret Primary School is a Rights Respecting School, the principles of equality, dignity, respect, non-discrimination and participation are at the heart of everything we do and these principles underpin our fundamental values. The policy is in line with:
Best interests of the child – The best interests of the child must be a top priority in all decisions and actions that affect children.
Right to education – Every child has the right to an education. Primary education must be free and different forms of secondary education must be available to every child. Discipline in schools must respect children’s dignity and their rights. Richer countries must help poorer countries achieve this.
Goals of education – Education must develop every child’s personality, talents and abilities to the full. It must encourage the child’s respect for human rights, as well as respect for their parents, their own and other cultures, and the environment.
Aims
This policy aims to ensure:
Legislation
This policy is based on requirements set out in the statutory framework for the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) that applies from November 2024.
We also make use of the non-statutory guidance provided in the ‘Development Matters‘ and ‘Birth to 5 Matters’ document to support and inform our EYFS provision.
Structure of the EYFS
Lady Margaret Primary School offers Nursery provision for up to 78 3-4 year olds. The maximum number of children that can attend a session is 39.
Children can attend nursery from the start of the term following their 3rd birthday. Admissions are managed by the school.
Children in the nursery should attend for a minimum of 15 hours each week; 3 hours each day as either a morning (8:30-11:30 am) or afternoon (12:30-3:30 pm) session. We do not offer 15 hours over less than 5 days.
Children can also attend for 30 hours each week: this can be funded through the government 30 hours scheme, or can be privately funded. We suggest that children attend for the full provision everyday, but part time 30 hour provision can be arranged if circumstances require this and there is space.
The school will consider providing a funded 30 hour place for children with social care involvement or where the family are facing significant issues.
The cost of an additional 3 hour session is: £17.00 per session. If the child is staying for lunch then the cost is £20.00 per session. This equates £100.00 per week.
If a child is accessing 30 hour provision and is staying at nursery for lunch, then there is additional fee charged to cover supervision over the lunch period.
Lunchtime supervision fee: £3.00 per day/ £15.00 per week.
30 hours provision is subject to spaces being available.
The cost of the food at lunch is NOT included in this fee.
Parents can either provide a packed lunch or can pay for a hot lunch with the school meal provider.
For full terms and conditions regarding nursery admissions and 30 hour places; please refer to Appendix 2.
There is currently no provision for nursery children in the before school club or after school club; however, this is reviewed regularly so parents should inform the school if this is something they require and it would be considered.
Parents should apply for a Reception place for their child in the autumn before they are due to start. Admissions are managed by Ealing Council.
Parents can apply to defer their child’s Reception start date and the school will support this where there is a strong reason to do so. The school may also suggest deferment to parents where they believe that the child would benefit from an additional year in nursery. If the school suggests deferment, then the child will receive a funded 30 hour place for their additional year in nursery.
Children starting Reception will attend for around 2 weeks on a shortened day to support their transition. Staggered start dates are given to new Reception starters.
Curriculum
Our early years setting follows the curriculum as outlined in the latest version of the EYFS statutory framework that applies from October 2024.
The EYFS framework includes 7 areas of learning and development that are equally important and inter-connected. However, 3 areas known as the prime areas are seen as particularly important for igniting curiosity and enthusiasm for learning, and for building children’s capacity to learn, form relationships and thrive.
The prime areas are:
The prime areas are strengthened and applied through 4 specific areas:
Staff plan activities and experiences for children that enable children to develop and learn effectively. In order to do this, staff working with the youngest children in our Nursery are expected to focus strongly on the 3 prime areas.
In Reception, a strong focus remains on the prime areas and in addition, the specific areas of Literacy and Numeracy.
Staff also take into account the individual needs, interests, and stage of development of each child in their care, and use this information to plan a challenging and enjoyable experience. Where a child may have a special educational need or disability, staff consider whether specialist support is required, linking with relevant services from other agencies, where appropriate.
In planning and guiding children’s activities, staff reflect on the different ways that children learn and include these in their practice.
Each area of learning and development is implemented through planned, purposeful play, and through a mix of adult-led and child-initiated activities. Staff respond to each child’s emerging needs and interests, guiding their development through warm, positive interaction.
As children grow older, and as their development allows, the balance gradually shifts towards more and longer ‘taught’ carpet sessions to help children prepare for more formal learning, ready for year 1. Teaching of the prime areas in reception involve a whole-class taught sessions, followed by group focus task led by an adult. Some sessions in the Summer term will be taught in a classroom with desks for every child to sit at.
All children in the EYFS will have the opportunity to access learning in the outdoor area every day.
We refer to the resources available at all times, including the actions and support of staff as ‘continuous provision’. The indoor ‘table’ activities and outdoor planned activities are referred to as ‘enhanced provision’.
Carpet sessions are also referred to as ‘taught sessions’.
In Nursery, a typical week will have daily taught sessions of rhymes/songs, phonics, read aloud, and fine/ gross motor activities.
They will also have maths, circle time and PE sessions each week. They actively care for our chickens and ducks.
In Reception, children have daily phonics, maths and core text/writing and fine motor skills/ handwriting sessions. They have one session per week of circle time/PSHE. Forest school takes place once every three weeks. Musical storytelling provided by ‘Everyday Magic’ and Music are taught every two weeks.
Understanding the World which includes the areas of curriculum that will be known as RE, Science, History and Geography is taught once a week through whole-class input, followed by group focus tasks throughout the week. This is further explored through enhanced provision. Expressive Arts and Design, known as Art and DT, are taught explicitly through a whole-class taught session at the start of a half-term, with a final project created by the end of the half-term as children work in focus groups. It is further explored throughout enhanced and continuous provision.
Children access daily activities that support all areas of learning and develop the learning introduced in the taught sessions through enhanced provision and real-life contexts.
To ensure that children are prepared for the learning they will do in KS1, children are taught identified key vocabulary and concepts as part of their taught sessions and this is reinforced in both continuous and enhanced provision and through taught sessions.
The school uses the Little Wandle Phonics Scheme.
Children in Reception attend Forest School regularly. This takes place off-site, on King George’s field adjacent to Durdan’s Park School.

Assessment
At Lady Margaret Primary School, ongoing assessment is an integral part of the learning and development processes. Staff observe pupils to identify their level of achievement, interests and learning styles. These observations are used to shape future planning. Staff also take into account observations shared by parents and/or carers.
In Nursery, children will be assessed using the I CAN Ages and Stages document for Speech and language development, and against the Birth to 5 Matters guidance within the first half term to establish a baseline and to inform planning and provision. This will then updated termly to track progress and identify where extra support may be needed. This is in addition to the ongoing assessment that takes place on a daily basis to inform the next steps for each child.
A class Learning Journey is maintained for Nursery and Reception in which a record of experiences and activities is kept. Whilst we recognise that this is not a statutory requirement, this Learning Journey provides a starting point for dialogue with children about their learning and a visual aid to support communication with parents.
Within the first 6 weeks of starting reception, staff will administer the Reception Baseline Assessment (RBA) to every child. Children joining at any point in the Reception year will be assessed within 6 weeks of the start date.
At the end of the EYFS, in the summer term of Reception, staff complete the EYFS profile for each child. Pupils are assessed against the 17 early learning goals, indicating whether they are:
The profile reflects ongoing staff observations and knowledge of the child, work completed by the child, and discussions with parents and/or carers. The results of the profile are shared with parents and/or carers for their child in the Summer Term report and with year 1 teachers at transition.
The profile is moderated internally (referring to the Birth to 5 matters guidance and to exemplification materials supplied by the DFE) and in partnership with other local schools, to ensure consistent assessment judgements. EYFS profile data is submitted to the local authority and shared with parents.
For an overview of assessment in the EYFS, refer to the EYFS overview of assessment document.
Meeting expected levels of development (‘expected’)
Not yet reaching expected levels (‘emerging’)
Working with parents
We recognise that children learn and develop well when there is a strong partnership between staff and parents and/or carers.
Parents and/or carers are kept up to date with their child’s progress and development. The termly parent meetings and reports and EYFS profile helps to provide parents and/or carers with a wellrounded picture of their child’s knowledge, understanding and abilities.
Each child is assigned a key person who helps to ensure that their learning and care is tailored to meet their needs. The key person supports parents and/or carers in guiding their child’s development at home. The key person also helps families to engage with more specialist support, if appropriate.
In Nursery, the key person will be either the class teacher; or one of the Nursery Nurses/HLTAs.
In Reception, the key person will be the class teacher.
Each term, parents will receive a written update on their child and also a 1:1 parent meeting with their child’s teacher. All parents will meet their child’s class teacher during the first two weeks of starting school. Other 1.1 meetings during the year will take place either during a designated parent’s evening OR alongside an ‘open’ session in school when parents are invited into the setting to observe and participate in learning activities alongside their child. When in person visits are not possible, then telephone or remote video meetings will take place.
During the summer term, the written report will be longer. For children in Reception, the outcomes from the end of year profile assessment will be shared with parents.
Parents are expected to have a working email address and to be able to access the key online platforms/programs that the school use to share online working. In addition, parents should be prepared to use Teams or Zoom for any online meetings or teaching. Upon entry to the EYFS staff will ask parents about their access to the internet and the devices they use to do this so that support can be given where necessary.
Safeguarding and welfare procedures
We promote good oral health, as well as good health in general, in the early years by providing activities that explore:
In addition, we will teach the RSE units of work provided by the school’s PSHE scheme, Jigsaw. Parents will be invited to view the content of these units before they are taught.
We follow statutory guidance for safety around supervised tooth brushing.
The rest of our safeguarding and welfare procedures are outlined in our safeguarding policy. See also the ‘EYFS policy for the safe use of mobile phones and cameras.’

This policy will be reviewed and approved by the Assistant Head of School (currently Miss Ali) every 1 year. Page | 7 At every review, the policy will be shared with the governing board.

English
We aim to ensure that every pupil leaves our school as a fluent reader, an articulate speaker and a confident writer, ready for the next stage of their learning journey.
Children should learn material by heart.
This gallery showcases our pupil’s work in English.
Writing
Writing sits on a sea of talk and we recognise the importance of separating composition and transcription for early writers. Once pupils have secured strong foundations, they move to a highly effective and well embedded writing curriculum, which uses high quality texts as models for writing. As a result our outcomes in writing are consistently significantly above national at the end of key stage 2.
In accordance with the National Curriculum, Lady Margaret Primary School believes:
Writing has a pre-eminent place in education and in society. A high-quality education in writing at Lady Margaret Primary School will teach pupils to write fluently so that they can communicate their ideas and emotions to others and through their reading and listening, others can communicate with them.
Through engaging in high-quality activities based around a high quality text, pupils have a chance to develop culturally, emotionally, intellectually, socially and spiritually. Literature, especially, plays a key role in such development. Pupils will also have acquired a wide range of vocabulary, an understanding of grammar and knowledge of linguistic conventions for reading, writing and spoken language.
Through the core texts selected and studied, the pupils at Lady Margaret will learn to appreciate our rich and varied literary heritage and by the end of their primary school journey pupils should be able to write clearly, accurately and coherently, adapting their language and style in and for a range of contexts, purposes and audiences.
The writing curriculum is carefully planned alongside the aims of the National Curriculum guidance for Key Stages 1 and 2 with clear progression across year groups. Pupils in EYFS are provided with every opportunity to engage in mark making across the curriculum. We separate transcription from composition for early writers. This means that early writers are given “golden sentences” which are dictated for them to secure their transcription skills. Alongside this we focus on high quality oracy opportunities to stimulate ideas for shared composition. Talk to stimulate ideas for writing is generated, in early years, through the use of role play, small world scenarios, helicopter stories and daily phonics sessions. Older children have access to drama, experiences and tools such as “conscience alley.” to stimulate ideas for writing. The curriculum is planned to ensure that a wide range of literature from different cultures and heritages is explored and valued.
We ensure that we establish and maintain high standards of handwriting and presentation, using the Nelson Handwriting programme. In early years, we use Occupational Therapy strategies to secure the correct pencil grip and develop finger strength. As pupils move through the school they taught to secure fluent, legible handwriting through frequent practice and specific teaching.
We have selected high quality core texts and created writing sequences whereby pupils are provided with opportunities to write for real purposes and real audiences. Our pupils have opportunities to apply and showcase their writing skills across the curriculum through a wide range of activities such as achievement assemblies, work of the week, poetry assemblies and “WOW” authors.
Together, we have designed the curriculum to best suit the needs of our pupils and to spark interest, challenge and curiosity. We teach writing alongside a different core text every half term which is often linked to the history/geography topics being studied. The writing sequences ensure:
Describe settings, characters and atmosphere in narratives.
Practice spelling words from the spelling list.
Handwriting Guidance for Parents
Top Tips for Practising Spellings
Reading
Reading is the cornerstone of our curriculum. This starts with a rich introduction to high quality stories and rhymes in early years and exemplary delivery of our phonics and early reading programme. High quality story times take place across the school alongside deep dives into a wealth of stories through the curriculum. Our approach ensures that every child develops a love of books and the skills needed to become confident, fluent readers enabling them to access the curriculum fully.
The Importance of Reading
Reading is a significant life skill and the development of reading strategies will enable our children to read and write confidently throughout their school career and on into adult life. Evidence suggests, that children who read for enjoyment every day, not only perform better in reading tests than those that don’t, but also develop a broader vocabulary, increased general knowledge and a better understanding of other cultures.
In fact, there’s evidence to suggest that reading for pleasure is more likely to determine whether a child does well at school than their social or economic background. At Lady Margaret Primary School we passionately encourage and require our children to read everyday and aim to nurture a love of reading through carefully selected texts, which inspire and motivate pupils to become life-long readers.
In early years, pupils learn to read accurately and fluently through daily phonics in reception and year 1, following the programme, Little Wandle Letters and Sounds Revised. They read regularly to adults through reading practice sessions using Big Cat decodable books and continue to develop their confidence in reading through repeated practice of the books at home. These reading sessions are designed to support children develop their fluency, prosody and comprehension. Children are also exposed to daily phonics, story time, focused story time reading sessions and opportunities for additional reading/phonics throughout the school day.
From years 2-6, children read as a whole class every day during English lessons. Reading and writing are both taught using teaching sequences which involve choral reading as well as opportunities for the teacher to read aloud, modelling expressive reading and for individual children to read aloud to develop their oracy skills and confidence.
Pupils’ comprehension skills are formally assessed termly. Any pupil who is not meeting age related expectations is support through additional sessions, 1:1 reading or phonics, small group reading/phonics and booster classes. Throughout the curriculum, pupils have a wealth of opportunities to learn and develop their reading skills as reading is a key feature of every lesson.
Pupils are encouraged to read widely through our use of carefully selected class texts, recommended reads, visits to the library and home reading practice books. Our classrooms and school reflect a literature-rich environment and we ensure reading is prevalent throughout the curriculum.
Our pupils are encouraged to read for pleasure and develop a life-long love of reading through practices such as: Every day, Every night (EDEN), reading partners, quiet reading time, engaging story times, reading challenges and working through recommend reads for their year groups. In early years and KS1, we also have Everyday Magic which promotes oral story telling.
In essence, pupils study a book, related to their half-termly topic, which is more challenging than those which they might be able to read independently. They will use this book as the basis for reading, writing, oracy tasks and links to foundation subjects. Year groups also have link texts to support their understanding of key themes and explore vocabulary further.
Click here for our core texts overview.
By the time our children leave Lady Margaret Primary School we aim for all of our pupils to leave as free, confident readers with a love of reading. Your child will be using their reading for learning across all subjects as well as for pleasure, and they will be developing their own reading tastes.
The emphasis is now on your child reading and responding to what they read accurately and quickly. They will be using accurate grammar and punctuation, as well as adventurous ideas, words, sentences, and paragraphs, to improve their writing as they draw on their wider reading experience. Your child should also be able to read and spell unfamiliar words using their knowledge of phonics and word structure. They will develop their spoken language through public speaking, performance, and debate.
We want the children to have a secure understanding of the different reading skills and know how to apply the reading strategies confidently.
Read to your childReading daily to young children, starting in infancy, can help with language acquisition and literacy skills. This is because reading to your children in the earliest months stimulates the part of the brain that allows them to understand the meaning of language and helps build key language, literacy and social skills. For an overview of our core texts please click here.
Sign up to your local libraryGet your child a library card. They’ll be able to borrow hundreds of fantastic books, and build up their “reading miles”. Let them choose what they want to read to help them develop their own interests
Tell stories togetherOne great way to introduce children to stories is to make them up together.
Model lifelong reading
If your child sees you reading they are more likely to want to read themselves.
Teach phonetic awarenessYoung children don’t hear the sounds within words. Thus, they hear “dog,” but not the “duh”-“aw”- “guh.” To become readers, they have to learn to hear these sounds (or phonemes). Play language games with your child. For instance, say a word, perhaps her name, and then change it by one phoneme: Jen-Pen, Jen-Hen, Jen-Men. Or, just break a word apart: chair… ch-ch-ch-air.
Listen to your child readWhen your child starts school, he/she will bring home two books; one selected from their weekly library visit which you should share together at home, and a second book which is pitched to their reading ability. We have an Every Day every Night (EDEN) programme, so we request that you take time to listen to your child read their book to you every day. Repeated oral reading is key to developing fluency.
Sign up for audiobooksAudiobooks are a fantastic way to for children to listen to stories. It allows children to listen to complicated topics and listen to better-quality books than your child might find at their own level. That exposure strengthens comprehension skills, particularly for children who have reading difficulties.
Ask questionsWhen your child reads, ask him/her to retell the story or information. If it’s a story, ask who it was about and what happened. If it’s an informational text, ask your child to explain what it was about and how it worked, or what its parts were. Reading involves not just sounding out words, but thinking about and remembering ideas and events.
All reading is good – Don’t rule out non-fiction, comics, graphic novels, magazines or leaflets. Reading is reading and it’s all worthwhile

Oracy
We aim to create a culture where every child's voice is valued and heard. Our pupils are given opportunities to talk, present and share ideas in every lesson enabling them to expand their vocabulary and to explore and deepen understanding across all subjects.
At Lady Margaret Primary School, we believe that oracy – the ability to communicate through speaking and listening – is just as important as reading, writing, and arithmetic.
We consider oracy to be an essential skill that supports children in every area of their education and prepares them for life beyond school.
Our aim is to ensure that every child has the confidence and ability to communicate clearly, express their ideas, and listen carefully to others.
We provide students with plenty of opportunities to practise these skills, whether through talk partners, debates, student-led assemblies, or our termly podcasts. These activities allow children to develop their speaking and listening abilities in a supportive, real-world context. In the classroom, we focus on helping students to become thoughtful speakers and listeners.
They are encouraged to take on different roles in discussions, such as explaining, listening, and challenging ideas, and to practise key skills like asking questions and building on others’ thoughts. By embedding these practices throughout their learning, we aim to give all children the tools to communicate confidently, respectfully, and effectively. We believe that by prioritising oracy, we are giving our students the skills they need to succeed both in school and in their future lives.
We aim for every child at Lady Margaret Primary School to leave Year 6 with the confidence and skills to speak and listen effectively in all situations. Oracy is at the heart of our teaching, ensuring that students develop the ability to communicate clearly, respectfully, and confidently across all areas of life.
By the time they leave us, students will be confident speakers, able to share their ideas in class, lead discussions, and present at assemblies. They will be active listeners, responding thoughtfully and respectfully to others’ perspectives. Our students will express themselves clearly, using appropriate language to explain, inform, or argue their points, and will ask insightful questions that deepen understanding and encourage meaningful conversation.

Geography
The curriculum for geography helps pupils make sense of the world around them and their place within it, they learn about local, national and global geography, exploring human and physical features. Linked to our theme of sustainability, we encourage respect for the planet and an understanding of environmental challenges.
A high-quality geography education should inspire in pupils a curiosity and fascination about the world and its people that will remain with them for the rest of their lives. Teaching should equip pupils with knowledge about diverse places, people, resources and natural and human environments, together with a deep understanding of the Earth’s key physical and human processes. As pupils progress, their growing knowledge about the world should help them to deepen their understanding of the interaction between physical and human processes, and of the formation and use of landscapes and environments. Geographical knowledge, understanding and skills provide the frameworks and approaches that explain how the Earth’s features at different scales are shaped, interconnected and change over time.

History
Our curriculum for history encourages historical enquiry and critical thinking. We aim to bring the legacies of the past to life and help pupils how it helps to shape the world today. We build chronological understanding through work on timelines, showing how historical events connect over time. Using our theme of power we consider how individuals and civilisations have affected change. Our goal is to inspire a lifelong interest in history, helping pupils to see themselves as part of an ongoing story, thus making the subject exciting and meaningful.
A high-quality history education will help pupils gain a coherent knowledge and understanding of Britain’s past and that of the wider world. It should inspire pupils’ curiosity to know more about the past.
Teaching should equip pupils to ask perceptive questions, think critically, weigh evidence, sift arguments, and develop perspective and judgement.
History helps pupils to understand the complexity of people’s lives, the process of change, the diversity of societies and relationships between different groups, as well as their own identity and the challenges of their time.
The national curriculum for history aims to ensure that all pupils:
At Lady Margaret School we teach history as a discrete subject but link it to our core text. This allows us to provide deep and wide-ranging knowledge whilst developing key skills and concepts in history.
The learning journeys in history are constructed through a set of learning statements that cover:
• Knowledge, understanding and concepts• Skills (working as historians)
Our History learning journey inspires pupils to have a curiosity and fascination about the history of the United Kingdom and of Ancient Civilisations from across the globe. Pupils will develop their sense of chronology and build upon their understanding from Key Stage 1.
Through studying the past they will develop a better understanding of the present. In developing their historical skills, concepts and knowledge they will be motivated to learn more about historical times and to develop an identity about themselves living in modern Britain.
Lady Margaret School serves a diverse community of many cultures and languages. We want all our children to gain knowledge and understanding of the history of this country and its relationships with the wider world.
We recognise that children at Lady Margaret live in a global city and should have the opportunity to learn about the history of London. Using this understanding, children as they grow older will have access to all the wonderful opportunities that the city has to offer.
Lady Margaret’s chosen Substantive Concepts
Substantive concepts are concepts concerned with the subject matter of history, such as invasion, trade, conflict, empire and monarchy. These concepts are woven throughout our history curriculum and are deliberately revisited in different topics to deepen understanding. Rather than teaching these ideas in isolation, they are explored through specific and meaningful historical contexts. This repeated exposure helps our children to build a richer understanding over time. Substantive concepts are considered generative knowledge because they help students make sense of new content. For example, once students understand the idea of trade in one unit of learning, they can apply that understanding to future units involving trade.
Although a wide range of concepts are explored, we focus primarily on these key ones, as we believe they are most relevant to the historical units we study

Mathematics
Our goal is to develop confident mathematicians who enjoy problem solving and see maths as a crucial tool for life. Concepts are taught in sequenced steps allowing pupils to build confidence and mastery over time
At Lady Margaret Primary School, we use Power Maths as a basis of our maths lessons. This is an exciting class mastery approach, which has been recommended by the DfE, (Department of Education) that works for every child. It is based upon the concrete, pictorial and abstract approach.
Every lesson is divided into sections that involve plenty of discovery, sharing, collaboration, practice and reflection.
Children are encouraged to solve problems each day through the use of concrete resources, pictorial representations and abstract thinking.
At the heart of this programme is the idea that all children can achieve and be successful mathematicians with the right growth mindset. It promotes five child-friendly characters, each with their own positive skillset, to inspire and motivate children.

By the end of Primary School, in Year 6, your child will have a good understanding of all the times table facts up to 12 x 12 and the following NC objectives:
Number and Place Value
• read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10 000 000 and determine the value of each digit• round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy • use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across zero• solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above.
Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication and Division
• multiply multi-digit numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using the formal written method of long multiplication• divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using the formal written method of long division, and interpret remainders as whole number remainders, fractions, or by rounding, as appropriate for the context• divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using the formal written method of short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context• perform mental calculations, including with mixed operations and large numbers• identify common factors, common multiples and prime numbers• use their knowledge of the order of operations to carry out calculations involving the four operations• solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why• solve problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication and division• use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Fractions (including decimals and percentages)
• use common factors to simplify fractions; use common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination• compare and order fractions, including fractions > 1• add and subtract fractions with different denominators and mixed numbers, using the concept of equivalent fractions• multiply simple pairs of proper fractions, writing the answer in its simplest form [for example, 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8].• divide proper fractions by whole numbers [for example, 1/3 ÷ 2 = 1/6 ]• associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [for example, 0.375] for a simple fraction [for example, 3/8 ]• identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places• multiply one-digit numbers with up to two decimal places by whole numbers• use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places• solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy• recall and use equivalences between simple fractions, decimals and percentages, including in different contexts.
Ratio and Proportion
• solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts• solve problems involving the calculation of percentages [for example, of measures, and such as 15% of 360] and the use of percentages for comparison• solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found• solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples.
• use simple formulae• generate and describe linear number sequences• express missing number problems algebraically• find pairs of numbers that satisfy an equation with two unknowns• enumerate possibilities of combinations of two variables.
• solve problems involving the calculation and conversion of units of measure, using decimal notation up to three decimal places where appropriate• use, read, write and convert between standard units, converting measurements of length, mass, volume and time from a smaller unit of measure to a larger unit, and vice versa, using decimal notation to up to three decimal places• convert between miles and kilometres• recognise that shapes with the same areas can have different perimeters and vice versa recognise when it is possible to use formulae for area and volume of shapes• calculate the area of parallelograms and triangles• calculate, estimate and compare volume of cubes and cuboids using standard units, including cubic centimetres (cm³ ) and cubic metres (m³ ), and extending to other units [for example, mm³ and km³ ].
Geometry – Properties of Shapes
• draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles• recognise, describe and build simple 3-D shapes, including making nets• compare and classify geometric shapes based on their properties and sizes and find unknown angles in any triangles, quadrilaterals, and regular polygons• illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter and circumference and know that the diameter is twice the radius• recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles.
Geometry – Position and Direction
• describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants)• draw and translate simple shapes on the coordinate plane, and reflect them in the axes.
• interpret and construct pie charts and line graphs and use these to solve problems• calculate and interpret the mean as an average.​

There is also a great focus on times tables at LMPS. Each year group has a termly baseline and end-of-term multiplication assessment – this helps us to identify pupils who have not secured the relevant multiplication/number facts for their year group. At the end of Year 4, pupils are required to sit an online Multiplication Tables Check.
The Multiplication Tables Check (MTC) is a key stage 2 assessment that tests pupils’ knowledge of all times tables up to 12 x 12. The purpose of the MTC is to make sure the times tables knowledge is at the expected level by the end of year 4. In years 5 and 6, pupils continue to consolidate their knowledge of the times tables up to 12 x 12.
